[[RunningHead]]

Part II: Touch

Susie Orbach

Susie Orbach

Susie Orbach  

That's my squeeze machine … some people call it my hug machine. … it exerts a firm but comfortable pressure on the body, from the shoulder to the knees.

As she lies in her machine … she feels that the machine opens a door into an otherwise closed emotional world and allows her, almost teaches her, to feel empathy for others.

(Oliver Sacks, An Anthropologist from Mars pp. 263, 264)

Psychoanalysis's Discomfort with Touch

Sometimes psychoanalysis comes to the ordinary common sense embarrassingly late. Tell someone not in the field that touch is crucial to human psychological and physical development and you'd get a contemptuous daa and yet we within the non-body, and particularly within the psychoanalytic, wing get singularly jittery and uneasy when touch comes to therapy. This can be the case even for those therapists who were trained in body therapies but whose current interests have led them to psychoanalysis. Indeed so uneasy are we about this, that we are either fuzzy and don't think about it or we have a set of rules around no touching as though that could resolve the issue. If we fall into the latter category, patients who touch us can become designated as rule-breakers and their wish to touch us or be touched by us can be interpreted callously as though their or our impulse were dreadfully wrong, pathological, boundary violating. By categorizing them in this way, we avoid engaging with what touch might be about. We move away from psychoanalysis's dictum to welcome and explore the meaning of things. Rather we can become threatened and deny ourselves access to crucial aspects of individual idiom, desire and need.

With a few exceptions, we psychoanalytic clinicians leave the discourse and theorizing about touch to the body-orientated therapists and we keep quiet about those hugs, the touch on the shoulder, the hand that needs holding, the kiss that got planted on us. In so doing we short-circuit an attempt to think about when and why we should or shouldn't touch. What are our and our patients needs, desires, fears of and confusions re touch? Unlike other psychoanalytic activities touch is just off limits.

Commentary by a French Psychoanalyst**

Janine Smirgel

Janine Smirgel

82 rue de l'Université, 75007 Paris

Janine Smirgel  

It is a real challenge to offer a commentary on clinical material of such concision, particularly when there is no available information on the process of the psychotherapy leading up to the present session. We learn however that the patient has cut down the quantity of medication being taken, which implies an improvement and a considerable investment in the object of transference (the psychotherapist). This human object, unlike the medication, has the capacity to abandon or disappear: the medication, as an inanimate object, is always accessible, and is therefore subject to control. It can be swallowed or left in the cupboard, which brings it into line with other objects of addiction (drugs, alcohol or food …). However, mention of the summer holidays immediately provokes the need for recourse to medication - an indication that the investment of the transference is not (yet?) accompanied by a stable internalization of the therapist.

In the present session, she [the patient] says: ‘If you put something in, something will come out’, as if it was impossible to keep the object.

The corresponding idea, that the patient does not want to be dependent on the analyst, comes out clearly in the session: she takes the wrong train, she does not take the lift (which is surely faster), all of which seems to indicate her ambivalence with regard to this session which precedes a week of absence. She admits: ‘I am worried about not being here until next Friday’. And when the analyst insists: ‘You're angry that you need to come and see me’, she replies: ‘I don't want to be dependent’. Dependence on medication (or, in other cases, on drugs or food) is in fact the result of a need not to depend on any human object.

The fears of abandonment are not surprising if one refers to her history: the loss of her father at the age of 4½, the fact that her mother had entrusted her to the care of her paternal grandmother, who seems to have been the most reliable and the most loving of the family, and the death of this grandmother. But the most serious abandonment that she experienced seems to be the moral one, by her mother, her elder sister (by ten years - thus a little mother?) and her brother-in-law. The latter, a father-substitute, abused the transference of which he was the object. The mother and the sister did not protect her from the brother-in-law. The sister acted in a ‘delinquent’ fashion, secretly administering medication to her husband. This is perfectly capable of provoking paranoid fears in the patient.

Commentary from A Group Analyst

Tim Woolmer

Tim Woolmer

IAA-trained group analyst 23 Kensington Square, London W8 5HN

Tim Woolmer  

It is no criticism to say of this piece that it feels so familiar. We've all been there, as clients and as clinicians. It is almost a stereotype of how things are, and all the more convincing for being so predictable. There is little to distinguish it from many other groups. This is how you would invent a fictitious first group, and it would not be ‘condemned as an improbable fiction’. It is the Ur-Group opening session.

Indeed, my first reaction was that there was little specific to comment upon. The presenter of the piece writes in the very first paragraph that this first session ‘contained all the anxieties and concerns that the text-books predict’. We are even told that the text-book was Yalom. And yet we know that this group, like every other, will go on to develop its own culture and unique history; even if we only get a hint at this early stage. As in a game of chess, there are relatively few legitimate moves but an infinite possibility.

So much for the first half of the first paragraph. The second half swings off at a tangent, and invites us to believe that individual and group therapy necessarily differ in their attitude to and treatment of dependency issues. It is a controversial claim at an inopportune moment.

Then we plunge into those familiar themes of the first group: names and introductions; silence and anxiety, not least the clinician's; a listing of problems; a searching for the rules; the first hesitant and covert attacks. The fact that it all feels so familiar is a tribute to the therapist, who keeps the group safe, while being aware of the potentials.

As I read the familiar litany, I found myself pondering three general issues about groups, as they implicitly arose in the story.

‘I think we are supposed to do it for ourselves …’ was a wonderful early sentence that indicated considerable sophistication, and it set me thinking about how far any group is a tabula rasa, and how far people arrive in groups with a knowledge of ‘the rules’, even while they may deny that knowledge. Where might such knowledge arise? I believe the answer is that we live in what might be called a ‘therapy culture’. For all the cynicism and indeed hostility to ‘therapy’ in its many manifestations, our culture has accepted therapy or counselling as legitimate, and has inserted it into our popular culture. The priest has made way for the counsellor in the popular imagination and most people have some idea of the rules of therapy. Our particular lexicon has been widely adopted. Most people, for example, have some idea what a Freudian slip is … or even what a group might offer. So we don't start from scratch, and we shouldn't underestimate what clients know when they arrive.

Attachment & Human Development5(1), 78-93, 2003

Using Attachment Theory to Understand Patients' Responses to a Therapist's Medical Break

Anne Power

The impact of a therapist's planned medical break is described and discussed, using attachment theory. The break is compared to Ainsworth's strange situation test and the responses of patients with avoidant, ambivalent and disorganized patterns of attachment are explored. The paper examines patients' responses at the point where news of the break is given and on reunion and looks at communication through breaks in the frame. An overview is given of the understanding of separation and loss in broader analytic theory and the ways in which these complement Bowlby's theory. The clinical cases are reviewed in the light of several authors.



Attachment & Human Development5(2), 97-119, 2003

Analysing Development of Working Models for Disrupted Attachments: The Case of Hidden Family Violence

Catherine C. Ayoub, Kurt W. Fischer and Erin E. O'Connor

This article offers a developmental model of attachment theory rooted in dynamic skill theory. Dynamic skill theory is based on the assumption that people do not have integrated, fundamentally logical minds, but instead develop along naturally fractionated strands of a web. Contrary to traditional interpretations of attachment theory, dynamic skill theory proposes that individuals continue to modify their working models of attachments throughout the lifespan. In particular, working models of close relationships develop systematically through a series of skill levels such that the skills vary across strands in the web and will not automatically form a unified whole. The continual modification of working models is particularly pertinent for the consequences of hidden family violence for individuals' development. Dynamic skill theory shows how trauma can produce not developmental delay or fixation, as has been proposed previously, but instead the construction of advanced, complex working models.

Responses to James Taylor and A.J. McGuire on Harold Bourne'S ‘A Homosexual Turns to Women’

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale  

Dear Editor

To bed past midnight, I unwrapped the latest BJP (Autumn 2003) and was startled, dismayed, flattered to discover myself solemnly designated a bad object for the psychotherapy readership. Next, however, it struck me as a bit rich to be abused as homophobic when I had been, way back when Taylor and McGuire were schoolboys if they were yet born, much involved in campaigning for homosexual law reform, well before Wolfenden.

What they find intolerable is anyone casting a clinical psychoanalytic eye on their sexuality and its purity, innocence and, above all, unquestionable health. Call it ‘same sex relations’ and there is nothing to puzzle about, or to make one stop and think and look deeper … let alone get worried and clinical! And whoever sees it otherwise is a benighted bastard who should be muzzled, censored, silenced - ‘unseemly in a learned journal’. Freud ran into this, of course, when he began to examine human sexuality, although political correctness had not yet been invented then nor had Freud-battering become an industry.

In fact, after dismissing my mild remark that most men turn to women sooner or later as a ‘crass generalization’ and omniscient pose, Taylor lumps my errors with Freud's - a compliment never paid to me before. He wouldn't be foaming at the mouth, you wouldn't be reading this, and I wouldn't be writing this if our Dads hadn't turned to our Mums. That's 3 out of 3 - 100% and very significant statistically. Yes, I insist omnisciently most men turn to women and therefore the planet is overpopulated.

Actually, by the time it appeared in print, numerous people had read my paper, among them homosexuals - one a psychotherapist, a few being patients, one the subject of the paper whose opinion I sought about it. It was years after the event and he wrote back, ‘That was me all right’, adding that he was now very different though somebody would probably identify him, which didn't matter if it helped others. With more therapy, he had become a family man with a prosperous business.

L.A. Confidential: Object Relations and Psychic Growth

Graham Clarke PHD

Graham Clarke

Graham Clarke  

Dreams are essentially … dramatizations or ‘shorts’ (in the cinematographic sense) of situations existing in inner reality … figures appearing in dreams … represent part of the ‘ego’ or internalized objects … therefore, the situations appearing in dreams represent relationships existing between endopsychic structures; and the same applies to situations depicted in waking phantasies.

(W.R.D. Fairbairn 1952, p. 99)

As has been argued elsewhere (Clarke 1994) one way of bringing an object relations perspective to bear on cinema is to see each film as representing the dynamics of an endopsychic structure. In this case all the characters in the film will be personifications of one or other dynamic structure as in the case of Fairbairn's derivation of the basic endopsychic structure from the content of a patient's dream (Fairbairn 1952). Fairbairn used three different approaches to the dream before looking at it as representing the dynamics of endopsychic structure and, similarly, any attempt to apply this approach to a film must recognize the plethora of other forms of analysis to which it might be subjected. Any film, like other real objects in the world, is capable of sustaining a variety of analytic responses. This is just one among many.

I want to illustrate the way in which this approach might be applied to film by looking at L.A. Confidential (1997, dir. Curtis Hanson, Warner Bros.) in some detail. My argument will be that there is a process of psychic growth depicted in the film through the doings and experiences of its three main characters - the only ones to be explicitly introduced to us as the film starts - Bud White (Russell Crowe), Ed Exley (Guy Pearce) and Jack Vincennes (Kevin Spacey). I suggest that each of these can be taken as a model for a possible central self but, as the film opens, each is flawed in some way. As the film develops each begins to grow and is transformed but, in the end, Vincennes is dead, White is immobilized and only Exley thrives. Exley has by now incorporated aspects of both Vincennes and White to become a more complete person and, incidentally, the exposer of and means whereby the L.A.P.D. rid themselves of a major corrupting influence in the form of Captain Dudley Smith, the internal saboteur (antilibidinal, over-rejecting ego). So, if we have three possible central selves each in their own way related to an internal saboteur, then what of the libidinal (over-exciting) self? In the classical oedipal triangle as represented by Fairbairn this self, or rather its object, is a woman. This woman is Lynn Bracken (Kim Basinger), a high-class prostitute and screen star look-a-like (Veronica Lake).

Challenges to Practice (Practice of Psychotherapy Series: Book One) edited by Bernardine Bishop, Angela Foster, Josephine Klein and Victoria O'Connell. Published by Karnac Books, London, 2002; 113 pages; £14.99 paperback.

Jo Robertson

Jo Robertson

London

Jo Robertson  

This is the first in a series of books exploring important and challenging issues confronting those working therapeutically in diverse settings. Drawing on the wide-ranging experience of members of the London Centre for Psychotherapy, the first volume concentrates on a number of new challenges to the classical psychoanalytic skills and techniques developed for intensive (three or more times per week) psychotherapeutic work. A forthcoming volume will consider contemporary ideas enriching psychoanalysis today. In light of this insightful, useful, first contribution, future volumes will be eagerly awaited by students and experienced practitioners alike.

As the crisis in modern-day mental health care provision deepens, there are many situations in which intensive psychoanalytic psychotherapy cannot be provided, is not wanted, or is not appropriate. (This is not to say it is neither needed, wanted, nor appropriate in a better world.) Each of the five chapters in this book seeks to address what is to be done in such circumstances, without compromising the professional integrity of practitioners often trained to respond solely within traditional models, who are perhaps made anxious when working outside such comforting ‘certainties’. Each chapter is informed by a spirit of modest, but thoroughly rigorous, enquiry:

We believe that by expressing our fears and doubts as well as our achievements we are not only describing our individual experiences but also are conveying something of the culture of the London Centre for Psychotherapy, which we value as a nurturing professional environment. (p. ix)

Josephine Klein's essay ‘When we counsel, analyse, therap’ establishes the ethical and theoretical framework for discussion in the entire book. She begins by pointing out that what the patient really requires is difficult in a first assessment to decide, and is rarely ever discussed, since practitioners tend to see what they have been taught to see, in accord with whatever training organization they attended, rather than looking with fresh eyes, expectantly, for the needs of their client to be revealed.

Clinical Commentary XXXI

I am grateful to Valerie Minogue for translating Janine Chasseguet-Smirgel's commentary and to all the contributors. One of my intentions in commissioning the authors was to explore the way clinicians from broadly similar theoretical positions (they themselves have determined how they wished to be described) would approach the same material. As it turned out, despite the proximity of their theoretical backgrounds, they have each brought a rather different approach to the clinical material.

Sue Robinson

Clinical Material

Clara is a young woman in her early thirties who came to this country from a neighbouring European country to work and to escape from a long history of sexual harassment and abuse from her brother-in-law. She is ten years younger than her sister who married when Clara was 12 years old. She loved her brother-in-law who during the courtship became a replacement father figure. Her father died when she was 4 years old. Her critical mother always worked and Clara was cared for by her paternal grandmother with whom the family lived. For the last six years of her grandmother's life Clara nursed her and has felt guilty ever since that she did not do more for her grandmother on the day of her death. Her grandmother died when Clara was 22. When Clara speaks of death she is tearful, and she fears the prospect of her mother's death. Clara's efforts to report the sexual abuse to the police resulted in her being asked to wear longer skirts, and in a policeman making advances to her as he drove her home. The reported sexual abuse took place from the age of 12 until the age of 24. Three times Clara moved out of home, but for various reasons was forced to return. Her sister and mother did nothing to stop what was happening, apart from her sister secretly administering medication to her husband by putting it in his tea.

Clara was put on anti-depressant and anti-psychotic medication at the age of 18 and has remained on it ever since. She has a strong attachment to her medication and, when she starts to panic, immediately checks to make sure she has taken her correct dose.

A Homosexual Turns to Women

Harold Bourne

Harold Bourne

Via P. de Cristofaro 40, 00136 Roma, Italy

Harold Bourne  

Most men turn to women, sooner or later, and in that regard my patient is unexceptional. Common as it is, however, the process seldom comes into clinical view, and so his particular experience of it may throw general light, even though (or perhaps, just because) it was more delayed and tortuous than usual. He achieved sexual intercourse with a woman when he was 21; for a few months earlier, he was a psychiatric patient; and before that, he had struggled since puberty against submerging amongst those who cannot turn to women - the minority we call homosexual.

My theme is how the female genitalia affected him, what his reactions were to intercourse, and why. For the purpose, I shall only require fragments of his life history and of the phase of psychotherapy before he managed coitus; most details, consequently, are omitted. In fact, it was only after the great event that my dealings with him began, since his treatment until then was conducted by my registrar at the time.

In the first place, he came to be a psychiatric patient because of the disastrous effects of attempts at heterosexuality. He found himself impotent; underwent a religious conversion which, for a while, safely prohibited further sexual adventures; grew attached to a girl whom he also brought to the Lord and whom, after barely three weeks, he resolved to marry; and, with that, psychotic symptoms overtook him in real earnest. Initially, he had gone for reassurance to his doctor and persuaded him frequently to examine his genitalia and once to obtain a semen analysis; later, when he began to be oppressed by sneers about homosexuality which friends seemed to be making, or perhaps Satan, he was referred for psychotherapy.

He was 20, a student, good-looking, and a nationally known athlete. He had the classic background for homosexuality - no memory of a father, a mother the widow of a short-lived marriage to a man 25 years her senior, and a steady homosexual relationship over three years in boyhood with a lodger aged 40 whom he had wanted his mother to marry.

Setting the Scene III: The Perspective of A Sympathetic Outsider

Alexander Layton

Alexander Layton

20 Essex Street, London WC2R 3AL. [email: alayton@20essexst.com]

Alexander Layton  

I am not going to attempt in these remarks to set out the law on confidentiality, but rather to offer one or two reflections from the perspective of a sympathetic outsider on the way in which the civil courts might approach issues relating to confidentiality in this area. Dr Hale and Mrs Garvey have given examples of what the law does and how it can operate in this field and, while some of what follows will touch on the law itself, I have necessarily simplified my account of the law and it should not be treated as legal advice. I shall confine my remarks to the common law and not attempt to grapple with issues such as data protection and access to medical records which have their own statutory regimes.

In general, English law will protect communications from disclosure if they have been made in circumstances of confidence. This applies if information is imparted confidentially or in circumstances which are such as implicitly to give rise to a relationship of confidence - such as would be inherent in a relationship between a psychoanalytic psychotherapist and a patient. There really is no doubt or argument about whether a patient's communications with a psychotherapist are confidential. They plainly are. The difficulties come in defining the boundaries of the confidentiality and, of particular concern, the circumstances in which the confidentiality will be over-ridden and disclosure will be required.

The paradigm case will involve a civil dispute in which the psychotherapist is called upon to disclose or confirm information or communications which he or she has received from a patient in the course of psychotherapy, or even the fact that a particular person has been receiving psychotherapy. This is perhaps the most likely context in which these issues will arise. But there are many others. It may unfortunately be a claim against, or even by, the psychotherapist.

An Evaluation of a Childrens' Drug Therapy Service

Bernie Carter

The small-scale evaluation of one initiative set up to try and support the children of parents who are the substance users is presented. The service, consisting of one worker, aims to safeguard and promote the child's welfare through direct work with children and their families and through liaison and collaboration with a range of professionals. Data were generated through a mix of semistructured interviews with key professionals and questionnaires distributed to professionals and parents currently using the service. The findings of the study demonstrate how professionals and parents perceive that the service reduces the social isolation the children experience and provides them with opportunities for sharing their experiences with a trustworthy adult and with other children in a similar situation. Parents report benefiting from the service through the support they receive outside mainstream drug, health and social services. Professionals benefit from the expertise that the worker has and the opportunity to work creatively with the children and their families.



International Forum for Psychoanalysis11, 264-274, 2002

Postmodernism: Its Origins and Its Threat to Psychoanalysis

Robert R. Holt

Postmodernism originated in an over-reaction to ‘modernist’ sociocultural trends of the past few centuries. Flaws of postmodern writers include: ignorance and distortion of the history of science and philosophy; the erroneous assumption that such faults of some natural scientists as reductionism and narrowness are intrinsic to the entire enterprise, even to rationality; overgeneralizing such valid criticisms to the level of metaphysical relativism; and deliberately obscure and pretentious writing. Its vogue is a threat to science in general and to psychoanalysis in particular. Psychoanalysis was vulnerable to a postmodernist attack because of Freud's rejection of scientific standards for his creation, his naïve realism, and his authoritarian heritage plus certain weaknesses of theory, technique and organization resulting from it. Analysts are urged to stay close to clinical observation and abstain from generalizing outside their realm of expertise.

Introduction

The current interest within our profession in issues of confidentiality reminded me of an address by Lord Bingham on that subject, written for an interdisciplinary audience (Inaugural Lecture of the National Council for Family Proceedings, 1996). Lord Bingham has generously agreed to revise and update ‘Confidentiality: an interdisciplinary issue’ for publication.

Whilst most readily comprehensible to lawyers, the address contains points of interest for psychoanalytic psychotherapists, notably his explanation of the frequently misunderstood term ‘legal professional privilege’ as well as his clarification of the rationale behind the usual requirement of ‘openness’ in court proceedings. By giving us the historical context in which our need for a measure of privilege comes to the fore, we are helped to understand the difficulties we face in our attempts to withhold evidence (or that which is perceived to be such by others). Although Lord Bingham's main focus is on children's cases, the legal references would be useful in alerting any lawyer we might consult to the issues involved (some colleagues' recent experiences would confirm that to be necessary), and it has relevance for us whether we are ‘Child’ or ‘Adult’ therapists. Adults are invariably involved in legal cases concerning children, whether as parents, carers, social workers or in various other capacities. As children are never called upon to be witnesses, adults fulfil that function. Any of us might have such a person as our patient.

This paper's interdisciplinary provenance is useful in encouraging us not to see the legal system or lawyers as unsympathetic to our position. It is understandable that those required to give evidence against their own best judgement feel bruised by the experience, but I have noticed a certain hostility towards legal issues amongst us, perhaps resulting from feeling threatened. The systems theory concept of the closed system is suggested by Ronald Fairbairn as one metaphor both for internal object relationships, and their expression in transference. This paper considers how this metaphor may be helpful in analysing the patient-therapist relationship and, particularly, in deciding when aspects of it should be understood as transference. The argument is that one major challenge could be seen as lying in the complexity and subtlety of internal world systems, and a second in the many factors that conspire to lure the therapist to participate in rather than notice them. The systems metaphor seems useful both in bringing into focus some of the difficulties in analysing the therapist-patient relationship and also in offering a vehicle for thinking about them.

The Complete Correspondence of Sigmund Freud and Karl Abraham edited by Ernst Falzeder. Published by Karnac Books, London and New York, 2002; 626 pages; £45.00.

Joseph Schwartz

Joseph Schwartz

London

Joseph Schwartz  

What a relief to read a calm, intellectually disciplined correspondence that highlights problems and prospects in psychoanalysis as experienced by the pioneers. In place of the overheated exchanges between Freud and Fliess, Freud and Jung and Freud and Ferenczi that have permitted hostile historians and others to play fast and loose with psychoanalysis as a misbegotten child, we have between Freud and Abraham a mutually respectful exchange of ideas, clinical problems and personal difficulties. Abraham addresses Freud as Professor throughout the years of a correspondence that includes frequent visits between the two men and their families in Vienna, Berlin and on holiday.

Abraham was no sycophant. When Freud taxed Abraham for his reservations about the staffing of a publishing project, Abraham responded (27 October 1923) angrily reminding Freud of past disagreements between them on personal matters. Freud's response in turn shows us a professional Freud acting as a colleague and not as a deranged lunatic as depicted in what Hanns Eisler has called the FBI, the Freud Bashing Industry, led by bashers like the Berkeley literary critic Frederick Crews and the psychiatrist Raj Persaud:

Let us not give too much play to the repetition compulsion. You were certainly right about Jung, and not quite so right about Rank. It does not have to be the case that that you are always right. But should you turn out to be right this time too, nothing would prevent me from once again admitting it.

Freud's correspondence with Abraham was far less intense than his correspondence with Jung, Ferenczi or even Jones. In the seven years before World War I, Freud wrote to Ferenczi every four or five days, to Jung once a week and to Jones three times a month. Freud corresponded with Abraham once a month - a sign of the more measured relationship between them.

Here is Abraham (3 June 1915) engaging Freud on ‘Mourning and melancholia’:

One other point remains: the postulation in your short manuscript that reproaches that are actually directed against another person are transposed to one's ego. I am not yet convinced of this. I do remember your bringing detailed proof in your paper. If it does not involve too much trouble, I should like to have a letter from you explaining more exactly what you mean and how you account for it.

James Taylor

James Taylor

15 Broomfield Crescent, Leeds LS6 3DD. [email: james.taylor@ntlworld.com]

James Taylor  

Dear Editor

As a psychotherapist, a subscriber and a contributor to your journal, I am writing for two reasons.

The first is to acknowledge and support your editorial note re the term ‘certain rabid Kleinians’ (BJP 19(3): 399). I am not a Kleinian but agree the phrase was indeed inflammatory and as you said ‘… not seemly for a learned journal’. The second is that I hope in a future journal you will be willing to publish a similar apology with regard to the article you published by Harold Bourne, entitled ‘A homosexual turns to women’ (BJP 19(3): 349-54). In my opinion his article is both heterosexist and homophobic and, thus, inflammatory and offensive. I will make what I hope will be sufficient points to demonstrate that the publication of the article was ‘… not seemly for a learned journal’.

My position is that, where conclusions as to anyone's mental health or illness are offered on the basis of their sexual orientation, what is communicated clinically serves to cover the prejudice of the clinician. Instead, I suggest that it is the quality of the client's object relations and their understandings of the world around them that assist us when we weigh up these matters. There is little explanatory value in generalizing anything from one badly, because partially, reported case and it is unhelpfully reductive to conflate sexual orientation or practice(s) with the related but necessarily more elaborate narratives that surround sexuality/sexual identity, gender and mental illness. What Bourne offers, by his own account, is a ‘Clinical Communication’ in which ‘most details … are omitted …’ (p. 349), and through which ‘… nothing really important had taken place’ (p. 354). From the outset of the treatment to its conclusion his patient clearly displays psychotic understandings of anatomy, sexing, gender and both same sex and opposite sex relations. Put another way, in spite of the treatment, he remains unable to symbolize and this inability causes him a variety of ongoing discomforts. What is alarming is that Bourne, in his zeal to fit his client into a less than persuasive account of so-called ‘castration anxiety’, acts out his own and possibly also acts in his client's homophobia.

Dear Editor

I imagine that others will have shared my disquiet in reading Harold Bourne's paper, published recently in the BJP (19(3): 349-54).

One had hoped that the attitudes towards homosexuality in Bourne's paper were things of the past; certainly, to read it is to enter the thought-world of the 1950s or 1960s. The outlook announces itself with the title: ‘A homosexual turns to women’. To take a related type of case, it is far from infrequent that a married man in early middle-age realizes, out of a deep and persistent distress, that continuing to deny his gay sexuality is an impossiblity, that he married chiefly because of societal pressures, and that wholeness and healing require an acceptance of his gayness. Would Bourne, one wonders, want to categorize that as ‘A heterosexual turns to men’? The assumptions being made by Bourne about sexuality show themselves, too, in such phrases as ‘submerging amongst those who cannot turn to women - the minority we call homosexual’, which indicates gay identity is being seen in terms of inability and lack of capacity. As well as this, there is the egregious presupposition that there is such a thing as a ‘class background for homosexuality’, something which no reputable scholar would now maintain.

The level of argument shown in Bourne's paper is routinely jejune. He produces, for example, elaborate hypotheses as to the significance of particular dreams and phantasies. Yet there is no consideration, or even apparent recognition, of the possibility that these dreams and fantasies can be just as readily analysed with conclusions diametrically opposite to those Bourne draws.

Response to Bob Hinshelwood, ‘Responsibility and Redress Revisited’

Carola Thorpe

Carola Thorpe

Flat 10, Old Court House, 24 Old Court Place, London W8 4PD

Carola Thorpe  

Dear Editor

Bob Hinshelwood is right to say (BJP 19(4): 541) that my suggestion, which was that we should inform the patients of a practitioner who is ‘struck off’ of his/her change of professional status, would not address the problem of the patients' transference in some cases (actually the ones that need most help). Nevertheless, I thought that it would serve better than no attempt at all to protect such patients. At the same time, our present non-interventionist policy leaves our professional bodies open to accusations of negligence with respect to a ‘duty of care’, with the consequent undermining of public confidence in our professional worth. My experience of a patient who remained with a therapist who was known to be abusive was that the intrusion of some reality disturbed the abusive symbiotic bubble and gave her emerging doubts some credence on which she built, and she was eventually able to break free. The process took quite some time. We are at the interface of internal and external realities and can only talk to that part of the patient's mind that is available at the time: but we are not in a position to know what that is. Of course, how one imparts the information needs to be very carefully thought out; and that might require a range of solutions depending on circumstances.

I welcome Bob's suggestion of contracts as an alternative but wonder if the profession has the will and the resources or even the ability to make it effective? Such a contract might have been signed in good faith, but when an embattled situation emerges resulting in expulsion, there is nothing to stop the practitioner changing his title slightly and joining some accommodating alternative treatment register, or no register at all and just continuing to practise. The onus would then be on the Registering/Training Body to enforce the contract by checking if that the person was practising and, if so, suing the practitioner. With the attendant difficulties, time and financial commitment that would entail, to say nothing of the anathema of such activities, would our profession be prepared to do this if not obliged to by law?

Lydia Garner  

This paper looks at some of the problems concerning access of black people to NHS Psychotherapy Departments. It examines some of the clinical issues that can arise in offering treatment to black patients, including racism. It argues that in addressing these issues improvements could be made to services, so that black people have a better and more equal chance (as compared to their white counterparts) of specialist psychotherapeutic help.

The term ‘black’ is being used in a broad context to signify different from white and to include African-Caribbean, Asian and mixed race people. These issues are inevitably emotionally charged and difficult to write about without stirring up uncomfortable feelings in the reader. As Bion (1962) understood, thinking is an emotional experience and, in thinking about race and inequalities in psychotherapy services, minus K can come into force - it can feel easier not to know. A clinical example is used to illustrate awareness of racism as an internal reality and that working with these issues helped to prevent the premature departure of a black patient from therapy.

Diana Birkett

Diana Birkett

London

Diana Birkett  

‘Relapse is the most common outcome of treatment in addiction’ (p. 117). Despite such trenchant opening lines (this one from a chapter on relapse prevention), this is by no means a pessimistic book. In assembling 13 chapters by various writers working in the field of drug and alcohol addiction, it attempts to construct a framework for understanding the causes and manifestations of addiction in psychoanalytic terms. The editors' aim is to reclaim this client group from the relative neglect it has received from the world of psychotherapy. (Oddly, since their high rate of diagnosis is much more recent, eating disorders seem to be exempt from this neglect.) Two main reasons are adduced for this: one is the tendency to see all substance misusers as the same, perhaps because of the convergence of their behaviours when under the influence of the drug (i.e. they are all manipulative and unreliable); and the other is the blurring of cause and effect: ‘There is a distinction between psychopathology as a background to the development of addiction, and psychopathology which results from addiction’ (Weegman, p. 84). Other obstacles to understanding, and therefore to the willingness to treat, have been the very small samples on which earlier writers based their theories of addiction, generalizing from one or two patients (Abraham 1908; Rado 1933), and their tendency to fit addiction into a single pre-existing diagnostic group (manic-depressive, borderline or narcissistic are recurring categories). Even when drawing heavily on Kohut's theories, Weegman states: ‘There is no general personality type for addicted individuals, though the wider notion of damage to and deficits of the self is one which can be applied to different personalities and temperaments. It is a structural concept’ (p. 49). Similarly, there is no one form of treatment which will suit all those who abuse substances.

The opening chapter by Arthur Hyatt Williams suggests that the drug is used as a container for a reality that is experienced as intolerable, and draws on Kleinian theory to explain the excessive moral and emotional polarities of the addict in terms of primitive splitting. Another of the myths he challenges is that the addict suffers from a weak superego; his experience suggests, on the contrary, that it is strong and punitive, and that drug-taking offers an escape from its demands. Subsequent contributors tend to draw less on conflict theory, and more on deficit models.

Editorial

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

[annscottbjp@aol.com]

Ann Scott  

Psychoanalytic work exists in a liminal space, one that is neither fully private nor fully public. It is my intention, as the Journal's new editor, to promote debate about this space - in both the fine grain of the clinical encounter, and the wider setting of the work, both professionally and socio-culturally. I take up this role within a very established journal; longevity brings both security and the need for introspection about our task as a journal, a continuing examination of our project. Bob Hinshelwood's first announcements for the BJP, nearly 20 years ago, tell us that ‘The emphasis will be on clinically oriented papers which concern the technique of analytical psychotherapy or that have theoretical implications’; an emphasis that Jean Arundale, who has edited the Journal for the last eight years, retained and refined. Clinical work - its vignettes, its larger arc - will remain at the heart of the BJP: as one patient movingly said to her therapist, reported in this issue: ‘You stepped into my cancer world and stood alongside me’. Such personal, immediate speech touches us by its very simplicity. But interpretation of clinical speech will vary, and I want to maintain another founding impulse of the Journal: ‘it will attempt to confront the problems that beset communications between various schools using different terminologies.’ So the Journal will offer a continuing engagement with difference: differences in thinking, differences in understanding. And with the organizational dynamics of the profession, both in its formal structures - extending Bob Hinshelwood's early editorial point that ‘The political life of the profession has been gathering momentum over recent years’- and its informal ones. Each part of the Journal plays its part in this engagement - not only the main articles but the Personal Views, Review Essays, Book Reviews, Correspondence, Responses, Clinical Commentaries, and Abstracts from Other Journals. As does each member of the editorial board. The editorial advisory panel, meanwhile, helps us to maintain standards in their assessment of papers submitted for publication.

Psychodynamic Interpersonal Therapy for Early Alzheimer's Disease

Eileen Brierley , Else Guthrie , Charlotte Busby , Fredrica Marino-Francis , Jayne Byrne and Alistair Burns

Alistair Burns

Oxford Road, Manchester M13 9BX. [email: elspeth.a.guthrie@man.ac.uk]

Alistair Burns  

Recent advances in the pharmacological treatment of Alzheimer's Disease has meant that the cognitive decline for patients in the early stages of the disorder can be delayed. The improved prognosis means that patients may have considerable insight into their illness for a much longer period, which may be emotionally distressing for themselves and their families. This paper describes the development of a brief psychological intervention, based upon psychodynamic-interpersonal therapy, for patients in the early stages of Alzheimer's Disease. The key components of the model include: picking up cues; staying with feelings; working in the ‘here and now’; negotiation; understanding, linking and explanatory hypotheses; metaphor; sequencing of interventions (i.e. picking up cues → staying with feelings → linking to interpersonal problems); and the development of a shared interpersonal formulation. The cases discussed in this paper are drawn from a pilot study of psychodynamic interpersonal therapy plus usual care versus usual care alone.

Confidentiality: An Interdisciplinary Issue

Lord Bingham

Lord Bingham

Lord Bingham  

Our system of Civil Justice in this country is underpinned by three rules, widely regarded as fundamental. The first is that justice should be administered in open court, under the eye of the public, and judgment given in terms which explain the reasons for his decision, enable the aggrieved party to assess the prospects of appeal and enable the public to debate the principles involved. The second is that the parties should, subject to certain well-established exceptions, disclose to each other all documents relevant to the issue the court has to decide, whether the documents are helpful to a party's case or not. The third is that the court should not in reaching its decision rely on any evidence or argument which the parties have not had the opportunity to address.

The rationale of these rules is not in any way obscure. One Law Lord said in 1913 that:

in public trial is to be found, on the whole, the best security for the pure, impartial and efficient administration of justice.1

Another quoted Jeremy Bentham:

In the darkness of secrecy, sinister interest and evil in every shape have full swing. Only in proportion as publicity has placed can any of the checks applicable to judicial injustice operate. Where there is no publicity there is no justice … Publicity is the very soul of justice. It is the keenest spur to exertion and the surest of all guards against improbity. It keeps the judge himself while trying under trial … The security of securities is publicity.2

Another Law Lord, more recently, said:

If the way that courts behave cannot be hidden from the public ear and eye this provides a safeguard against judicial arbitrariness or idiosyncrasy and maintains the public confidence in the administration of justice.3

One of the outspoken critics of Lord Woolf's Interim Report based his criticism on the extent which the proposed reforms undermined the principle of public justice.4

The paper was presented at a public lecture organized by the National Council for Family Proceedings in 1996 and revised by Lord Bingham and Akash Nawbatt, Barrister, in July 2002.

Relational Dynamics in the Family

Parallel Psychotherapy with Children and Parents by Barbara Piovano (New Jersey: Jason Aronson, 1998; 216 pages)

Angela Joyce

Angela Joyce

21 Maresfield Gardens, London NW3

Angela Joyce  

Parallel Psychotherapy with Children and Parents is an account by an Italian psychoanalyst and child psychiatrist of her development of a model for treatment of predominantly severely disturbed children and their families in both a private and public health setting. In many ways it could be said that this book is truly innovative as it shows the author's learning from her experience and in so doing pushing back the frontiers of the method of treatment as well as her conceptual understanding of the territory in which she is working. She is open to new ways of intervening as well as understanding and thus shows herself to be a true researcher, prepared for her previously held assumptions and ways of going about treatment to be replaced by something new and different.

Barbara Piovano describes her pioneering model of the parallel psychoanalytic psychotherapy for the referred child and parent (usually the mother) in a publicly funded child guidance setting where the psychotherapists were then jointly supervised. It was later extended to use within private practice where Piovano brought together a number of therapists trained in child and adult psychoanalysis. The field thus created reflected and allowed expression of the relational dynamics within the family in such a way that they could be considered and worked with by the team of psychotherapists and supervisor. Traditionally this would have been seen as risking ‘contamination’ of each treatment by factors extraneous to that setting, which was protected so that the transference-countertransference matrix was most purely available for interpretation. Piovano argues most cogently that the field opened up is truly a reflection of the individual and family to be treated. She invokes Winnicott's notion of transitional space to capture both its creative and therapeutic potential. Clearly, in my view, it has to be used with care if the possible pitfalls are not to undermine the process through the contamination suggested.

This model would require an integrated team who could trust one another, risk mistakes and criticism as well as consider the dynamics of their own relational field so that the contamination by the family pathology would not used as an easy way out of grappling with the team's pathology. The investment in training and sustaining such skilled therapeutic staff would require a health service infrastructure that truly valued the potential power of these interventions.

Mark Linington

Mark Linington

London

Mark Linington  

There cannot now be many psychotherapists not influenced in their clinical practice by attachment theory. In his third book about the subject, Jeremy Holmes makes a comment early on that ‘these days attachment seems to be on everyone's lips’ (p. xi). Attachment theory is certainly a hot theory, growing fast, with multiple places of development and cultural influence. Holmes considers some of these developments, particularly those in psychological research, and turns them into something psychotherapeutically useful. As he puts it, his ‘perspective is unashamedly clinical’ (p. xi). He enlarges the vocabulary we have available to think and talk about what attachment theory means for our clinical practice. This is a useful thing to do because, although attachment theory is an increasing part of our clinical conversations, its range of implications for our psychotherapeutic practice still remain to be understood.

We might imagine that the importance of attachment theory is by now apparent for psychoanalysts too. However, the first title for this book which Holmes quickly rejected was ‘Why I am not a Psychoanalyst’: rejected because of its antagonism to the integrative aim of this book: to add something curative to the historical schism between intrapsychic psychoanalytic theory (particularly that of Melanie Klein and her followers) and the more environmentally concerned attachment theory pioneered by John Bowlby. Like Fonagy (2001) in his recent book, Holmes sees this as the historically correct time for a ‘rapprochement’ between psychoanalysis and attachment theory. And he may be right. Although perhaps the practice of all of us has never been as unadulterated by other ways of thinking, as the myth of the split would have us believe. Holmes has heard the story of this troubled relationship as a narrative of avoidant attachment. He seeks to ‘break open the narrative’ of our theory and practice to develop it into something that is ‘new and less constricted’ (p. 82).

The most innovative aim of the book is the development of the attachment theory of narrative. Holmes does more than re-present the theory of narrative from the Adult Attachment Interview (AAI). He takes the AAI's demonstration of a link between attachment patterns created in our earliest relationships and style of narrative in adult life, and develops a novel theory for thinking about the stories we hear in psychotherapy.

Dilemmas in the Consulting Room edited by Helen Alfillé and Judy Cooper. Published by Karnac, London and New York, 2002; 199 pages; £22.50 paperback.

Marguerite Valentine

Marguerite Valentine

39 Womersley Road, London N8 9AP, Arbours Association of Psychotherapists, Member of the Inner City Centre

Marguerite Valentine  

As psychotherapists we face challenges on a daily basis. Often these deny categorization, since they occupy an interface between theory, technique and the personal capacities of the psychotherapist. These challenges however represent a potential, since the therapist is called upon to respond uniquely to the specificity of the relationship constructed with a patient. This book is about these dilemmas and represents the thoughts and practice of a variety of clinicians, all of whom adopt different theoretical and clinical approaches to their work.

In their introduction, the two editors, Helen Alfillé and Judy Cooper refer en passant to the increasing rigidity and institutionalism of the practice of psychoanalysis. Within this, though this is not a point the authors make, there is a fear of not practising correctly, and thereby presumably facing the censure of one's colleagues and one's supervisor. As they point out, there are no absolutes. Yet since the practice of psychoanalytic psychotherapy is built on a relationship between two people, necessarily there need also be a space for the therapist's response to the dilemmas faced in the consulting room. It is this which forms the underlying theme in this book of readings.

Though the authors of these papers are in the main graduates of the British Association of Psychotherapists, they express a diverse and eclectic position towards the issues which they address. Some, such as the paper by Susan Lipshitz-Phillips on ‘Some thoughts on the use of the setting in psychoanalytic psychotherapy’, draw heavily on Freud and Klein yet, given the subject matter, I was surprised the author omitted the work of Winnicott (1990a, b). Similarly Simon Archer writing on ‘Violence and hostility from a sense of unconscious shame: shame in the countertransference’, where one would expect a reference to Kohut (1994) he draws primarily on drive-orientated theories. One wonders given this author's dependency on meta-theory how this comes to be translated into interpretations or used in a dialogue that is perceived as useful by the patient.

Responsibility and Redress Revisited

R. Hinshelwood

R. Hinshelwood

R. Hinshelwood  

Dear Editor

Carola Thorpe (BJP 18(1): 144-7) raises important issues about the unconscious dynamics in matters of confidentiality, and of a therapist's unfitness to practise. Using the Wynne Godley case she points out that he was in no position as a regressed patient to make sensible decisions about his analysis or analyst. This is a difficult, and perhaps common, problem associated with transference. Freud counselled his patients not to make important life decisions whilst in analysis. And therapists are counselled to beware of this kind of regression - which presumably Masud Khan did not heed.

When a therapist is so unethical or unprofessional as to be barred from membership of his organization, then what is the ethical responsibility of the organization? Carola Thorpe believes that the organization should inform patients of their therapist's debarment. This sounds harsh but in a way realistic.

However, some patients must be judged as incapable of making good decisions on the basis of reality, even when informed of it. Also I question Carola Thorpe's suggestion to compare the situation to when a therapist dies or becomes disabled? An abusive therapist is not dead and cannot easily be prevented from continuing his practice, in the way that death would prevent him! So, simply to inform patients might absolve the organization, but it does not fully address the problem, i.e. the patient's problem of his transference. Despite her integrity in facing and raising these issues, her solution may not be adequate.

Of course, it is hard to see what else could be done - other than requiring the debarred therapist to stop practice with his patients. However, once removed from his organization, the organization has no authority to stop the therapist. In this sense we are handicapped compared to the medical and nursing profession, where it is illegal to practise if removed from the statutory register (and also compared to psychotherapists in some other countries). It would seem this is another urgent factor in our need for that register.

Editorial

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

annscottbjp@aol.com

Ann Scott  

Themes of discomfort and bewilderment are at the forefront of this issue of the Journal, along with the ideas - sometimes innovative, sometimes traditional - that can support the clinician in bearing with and processing the difficulties of the work. As a colleague of mine said recently, ‘practitioners need holding as much as their clients’, and I hope this issue will contribute to such holding.

In a strong challenge to mentalism, with its ‘over-validation of mind and thinking’, Susie Orbach extends her longstanding interest in body countertransference to a consideration of the body in the consulting room. She proposes that we address the body on its own terms rather than solely for what it symbolizes, in order not to miss crucial dimensions of patients' experience. An exploratory discussion of touch (that is, the classical taboo on touch) follows. Orbach is supported by the framework provided by the John Bowlby Memorial Lecture and Conference in this endeavour.

Commentary from A Group and Jungian Analyst

Meg Sharp

Meg Sharp

88 Montagu Mansions, London W1U 6LF

Meg Sharp  

The group therapist has to be a dynamic administrator responsible for creating and maintaining the setting, monitoring and protecting the boundaries and, simultaneously, has to undertake a therapeutic role, leadership, analysis, interpretation. The first session is a critical time in any group. The early developmental or formative process, dealing with issues of being together, who's who, what resources are there, what is the task, what are the rules, and so on, is uppermost in the group therapist's mind. The task at this stage is to observe members' entry into the group, to establish ground-rules and boundaries and to provide a good container for whatever feelings may surface, at the same time allowing room for movement and flexibility whilst maintaining boundaries. This is the time to listen carefully, to learn, to wait, to hold and to let things emerge whilst learning the group language (and each group has its own). Containing one's own anxiety, always there at the beginning of a new group, and dealing with the new group's anxiety is a formidable and exacting task.

It is good preparation to see each member a few times before the start. Although we have little detail about the background of the individuals and even less about the therapist's own feelings before and during the session, early anxiety is evident. For example, the therapist stating his/her name and the group times presumably is an indication of this as the patients have already met the therapist. I have always found Foulkes' dictum of ‘go in, sit down and keep quiet’ very useful. The therapist's comments start off the group and set it on a similar route: ‘Are we supposed to introduce ourselves?’ Might the group evolve in another direction if the therapist had said nothing?

Commentary from A Kleinian Analyst and Group Analyst

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Colchester CO4 3SQ

Bob Hinshelwood  

As the therapist says, this clinical material shows all the characteristics of the first session of a therapeutic group. The levels of anxiety and bewilderment not unnaturally overwhelm everyone, perhaps even the therapist. I will try to describe what I see as the members' reactions, and then a few remarks about the therapist and the way he copes with this nearly impossible situation. (I realize that the therapist may be a woman, but for simplicity's sake I will refer to the maleness of the therapist.)

Much of the session is taken up with the members talking about the feeling of not knowing each other, and of bewilderment with the setting. There is an expressed annoyance with the therapist who is made responsible for their discomfort. We can see the annoyance as a reaction to the familiar sense of bewilderment and helplessness in an initial session, expressed here in Jane's initial confrontation with the therapist, ‘What's the point of coming …’ etc. However, this annoyed reaction is deftly undercut by Toby's guess that ‘We're supposed to do it ourselves’, a sentiment which goes some way to build up a bit of confidence that they are not as helpless as they feel.

The bibliography of the impressive book, Therapeutic Care for Refugees, No Place like Home, lists a page and a half of publications by the editor, Renos Papadopoulos, on the subject of refugees over 15 years which is evidence of the length and the depth of his involvement in this client population. This time he has assembled a group of distinguished researchers, clinicians and academics connected, as he himself is, with the Tavistock Clinic, who work with refugees either in the country of resettlement or in the territory of origin and are tackling different aspects of this new therapeutic specialism which has come to the fore in the profession since the war in the Balkans. There have, of course, been refugees since time immemorial, who had to leave their homes and resettle in strange countries to start new lives. These days refugees have become a big subject in the media and in the politics of this country and no-one can remain unaware of their presence. That they are also beginning to feature in the training of therapists and counsellors is largely due to Renos Papadopoulos, who is a refugee himself from Cyprus, and has drawn attention over the years by his prolific writing to the plight and the needs of his fellow-sufferers; in particular, but not exclusively, to their therapeutic needs which are central to this book.

Encountering the Shadow in Rites of Passage: A Study in Activations

Ann Casement

Jung's concept of the shadow is explored in this paper through his writings on its realization and assimilation in which he says the shadow may be experienced as the regressed and denied ‘other self’ in each individual. However, this is not the whole picture, and he also points to the fact that the shadow contains more than something merely negative. While in no way treating them as ‘patients’, the paper will also touch on the experience of the anthropologist, Bronislaw Malinowski, and the writer, Joseph Conrad, in their personal encounters with the shadow. All three encountered the shadow whilst going through rites of passage of their own and each owes much to the Romantic Movement. In this context, attention is directed to the writings of the philosopher and theologian, Johann Gottfried von Herder, who discovered a deeper understanding of his destiny in the course of a sea voyage.



Journal of Analytical Psychology48, 145-169, 2003

Daimonic Elements in Early Trauma

Donald E. Kalsched

This paper explores some of the ‘daimonic’ elements of unconscious mentation that emerge both in dreams and in the transference/countertransference field with early-trauma patients and illustrates these with an extended clinical example. An archaic and typical (archetypal) ‘trauma complex’ is articulated (with diagram) as a bi-polar structure consisting of divine child protected and/or persecuted by an inner ‘guardian angel’. Sources of this structure and its mythological inner objects are traced to trauma at the stage of what Winnicott calls ‘unintegration’ and to flooding by disintegration anxiety at a time before nascent ego-structure has formed.

In an extended case example, the author shows how the patient's traumatized innocence and desire for a new start, thwarted by self-attacking defences, pulls him into playing the inflated role of her guardian angel, leading to re-traumatization in the transference. Working through is seen as the necessary disillusionment and humanization of these daimonic structures as they are projected, suffered, and transmuted by the analytic partners in the stormy process of psychotherapy.

Editorial

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

[annscottbjp@aol.com]

Ann Scott  

The Journal is delighted to be publishing the Proceedings from ‘A Question of Confidence - Privacy Under Pressure’, the British Confederation of Psychotherapists' conference on confidentiality in March 2003. The papers make a crucial contribution to furthering debate in this area. A striking feature of the conference was the radical and challenging mix of papers: conference members had an opportunity to think not only about external relationships with the judiciary and the State, but internal relationships and the nature of the profession, in a way which allowed for the complexity of relations of confidentiality to be held fully in mind.

Following Coline Covington's introductory comments on background and context, the first group of papers, oriented to but not limited to considerations of the external world, cover the work of those clinicians and lawyers who are working with government on public policy and disclosure: Rob Hale, Pip Garvey and Alexander Layton QC. The first three speakers provide an invaluable account of the state of play in respect of official debate and of work in progress both clinically and politically, and consider what might be the most appropriate frame of mind from which to approach questions of disclosure. The second group of papers juxtapose two very different perspectives on psychoanalysis as a profession: those of Christopher Bollas and David Tuckett. While both offer an extended critique of the institutional dynamics and group relations of the profession, they have different readings of transparency as a goal for the profession, and of the nature of psychoanalysis as a treatment. Bollas's comic riff - the comedy of audit and disclosure which begins and ends his paper and had the audience in stitches - served only to underline the utter seriousness of his central point: ‘What is psychoanalysis? What does it claim to do? For what could it be held accountable, in what way, and by whom?’ Equally serious was David Tuckett's argument that the setting for clinical work depends in part on the way the discipline is viewed in the public mind and hence in the mind of the patient, paving the way for his proposal of a ‘BCP patient contract’.

[[RunningHead]]

Setting the Scene I: From Common Law to Statute Law

Rob Hale

Rob Hale

8 Fitzjohns Avenue, London NW3 5NA

Rob Hale  

This is an account of the talk that I gave at the BCP conference on confidentiality. It is personal and, at times, journalistic, and concerns itself with much that is political.

My own experience started some eight years ago at the Portman Clinic - an NHS psychotherapy clinic for people who have committed criminal or sexually deviant acts and are troubled by it. Paedophilia, for example, is a common reason for being referred. Not surprisingly, issues of confidentiality are crucial for such patients - most would like the assurance of absolute confidentiality. The extent to which we could (or should) provide such assurances was unclear to us. We therefore decided to consult two lawyers who gave us largely dramatically opposed opinions. This was the first lesson - that the law is not always clear and that it is subject to interpretation. The second is that there was often room for manoeuvre within the law, and hence the need for the professions to take an active (or proactive) role.

In this consultation we were made aware of the crucial difference between (i) statute law which is laid down by Act of Parliament, an infringement of which has specified punishment attached, and (ii) common law in which an individual (patient) who has a grievance against a professional asks a court to decide whether that professional has discharged his/her professional duty. Such a judgment would largely take into account the opinions of other members of that profession. The result would be that, if successful, the complainant would be awarded damages and the professional might be reported to his/her professional registration body.

The sanction of a professional body would be to deny the professional the right to work (being struck off or suspended from a register). An employing authority equally may decide that an employee has contravened its code of practice and terminate employment. Both registration authorities and employing authorities will have codes of practice.

Postscript: BCP Introductory Statement on Confidentiality

Following the BCP conference on confidentiality, the BCP Working Group on Confidentiality produced an ‘Introductory Statement on Confidentiality’ (July 2003). This is a working document that states the position of the BCP on the issue of confidentiality of clinical records. On the basis of this statement, the Working Group will be producing guidelines for BCP members on good practice including how and what information is kept on patients and what practitioners need to know about the Data Protection Act.

The constituent members of the BCP attach the highest importance to the maintenance of confidentiality in the communications between patients and their psychoanalyst or psychoanalytic psychotherapist and also in the privacy of any written notes.

The need for confidentiality in psychoanalytic work is akin to, but goes well beyond the need for medical confidentiality generally and beyond that required by psychiatrists, psychologists, psychotherapists and others who treat emotional and behavioural disturbance. The ethical codes of each of the professional groups contain statements about confidentiality relevant to their practice and some professional organizations provide guidelines for their members to follow. Central to the psychoanalytic approach is the exploration of interpersonal processes with attention to underlying unconscious activity. Very strict confidentiality is an essential prerequisite for the focus on and the use of this material. The disclosure of such material to third parties can be acutely damaging to the process and should be resisted in nearly all circumstances.

Psychoanalytic Confidentiality

It is recognized that confidentiality in psychotherapeutic work has a particular clinical importance. The decision of the United States Supreme Court in Jaffee v. Redmond 518 US 1 (1996)1 that ruled against the disclosure of a psychotherapist's notes is a case in point. The court there noted that treatment by a physician for physical ailments can often proceed successfully on the basis of a physical examination based on objective information supplied by the patient, and the results of diagnostic tests, but that effective psychotherapy, by contrast, depends upon an atmosphere of confidence in which the patient trusts the psychotherapist's commitment and capacity to protect their frank and complete disclosure of facts, emotions, memories and fears.

Understanding Consciousness by Max Velmans. Published by Routledge, London, 2001; 308 pages; £17.50.

David Black

David Black

London

David Black  

There is a real difficulty in talking about the new version of psychology which has become possible over the past two or three decades. It is that one is required to know too much, and to speak too many different ‘languages’. We have to be able to understand hard science (neuroscience, genetics), manipulate the intangible concepts of ‘soft’ science (cognitive and developmental psychology), be in sympathetic touch with emotion and phantasy (psychoanalysis and the psychology of groups) - and, at the same time, try to preserve some common sense as we move about among all these demanding systems of thought.

Perhaps this new territory should properly be called anthropology rather than psychology. For the first time, we have the prospect of a science which truly does justice to the complexity of human beings; but to get it into manageable form we will need to think about its many constituents with a freedom from prejudice that is still rare. In particular, the prejudice against philosophy that many scientists permit themselves will have to be abandoned.

Max Velmans's Understanding Consciousness is an excellent example of what can be achieved when these difficult requirements are met. Its title, both modest in form and huge in ambition, is a fair guide to his approach.

He begins with a very thorough and thoughtful review of the existing accounts of consciousness, particularly those by neuroscientists and cognitive and behavioural psychologists, and maps them onto the age-old philosophical discussion of the nature of mind. He shows very clearly how many modern debates are re-workings of traditional issues, and he usefully distinguishes the different sorts of dualist theory - substance and property dualism - and the different sorts of monism - idealism, physicalism, functionalism and dual-aspect monism. His careful sorting-out of the strengths and weaknesses of each of these positions is a model of clarity, and shows convincingly why the theories of, say, Francis Crick and Daniel Dennett (‘physicalists’) or of most modern cognitive psychologists (‘functionalists’) are inadequate to describe the unparalleled phenomenon of consciousness that we actually live with.

Herbert Hahn  

All five contributors to this engaging book have staffed the pioneering WPF Counselling and Psychotherapy Training in Supervision. The authors offer a good range of theoretical underpinnings, and vivid examples from their wealth of experience, in a way which illuminates theory and practice. The book is built on a broad and informed pluralistic analytic framework. Three of the authors are experienced analytical psychologists, and the other two are psychotherapy members of the FPC. Five of the chapters are separately authored by the two editors, four by Gertrud Mander, two by John Stewart, and one by Mary Banks, and the contributions are set out in four sections, with a degree of healthy overlap. The first three sections deal with the supervisory relationship in its various contexts, and ways of understanding and implementing the requirements of a formal training. The fourth and final section, headed ‘Generic Issues’, deals with ethics, supervision of supervision, and endings.

At the outset, Christine Driver lays out the orientation and content of the book in the form of a contract, which she compares to the commencement of therapy or supervision. She engages with her readers as an adult to adult level in a way which also encourages thought, reflection and stock-taking in relation to the reader's own position and what might be wanted or hoped for from the book. In due course the other authors convey the way in which they each both respect and value adult level of exchange in the supervisory relationship, while attuning to the ubiquitous range of underlying dyadic, oedipal, sibling and peer dynamics.

Edward Martin begins the first section by exploring and elaborating ways of listening to the absent patient. He also transcends the tramlines of current conventions by inviting us to reconsider the value of the original model followed by the Hungarian Psychoanalytic Society (as well as in Britain until 1947). In this, trainees were analysed and supervised by the same person. He wonders encouragingly about the possible current relevance of applying the idea to post-training supervision. This would imply a supervisor also holding a therapeutic brief or vice versa.

Judy Parkinson

Judy Parkinson

London

Judy Parkinson  

This short book was conceived, written, edited and illustrated by the Symington family, Neville and Joan Symington, both practising psychoanalysts, and their two sons. Neville Symington's text is very well illustrated by his wife's graphic cartoons.

There are six chapters, closing with a short glossary of psychological treatments and preceded by an introduction. Neville Symington states that the

244

book has been written for patients. This could apply either to someone looking for a psychotherapist or someone already in therapy but for whom the therapy is not working. He explains that the Western world has seen a huge growth in the number of counselling and psychotherapy trainings, and that practitioners abound, within a culture that anticipates and expects the meeting of individual emotional needs. Psychotherapy and counselling serve a population which, unless guided, may not know where to look for, or how to discern, a good practitioner and, unfortunately, standards of training are very variable.

The book is written in simple jargon-free language that will easily be related to by the layman, but which also conveys the seriousness with which Neville Symington approaches his subject.

At the beginning of the first chapter, entitled ‘The purpose of psychotherapy’, he states clearly that the aim of psychotherapy ‘is to cure sickness of the mind’ (p. 3). This, to my mind, helpfully sets the practice of psychotherapy within a context which differentiates it from a talk with a friend and separates ‘something quite mild’ (p. 4) from

the something that may be more serious: A patient may be suddenly overcome by a deep and terrifying sadness which has no apparent cause. … The person finds he cannot think properly, cannot remember things or finds that he has forgotten how to drive. … Something like an explosion has gone off inside him and all he knows is the effects. (pp. 4-5)

Reading these words, perhaps as someone suffering in this way and looking for help, I would feel taken seriously and relieved that my state of mind could be recognized and understood. I would feel similarly if I were an artist or writer and was finding that my creativity was blurred or paralysed, for no obvious reason. Symington is concerned both with the person caught in the throes of serious mental disturbance and the person who is just not functioning properly. ‘In the case of someone who has had a serious mental collapse good psychotherapy can help to reverse the situation and turn it into a new beginning’ (p. 10). Equally, ‘psychotherapy is concerned to bring someone to his full potential’ (p. 10).
